content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to learn adversarially robust representations that are task-agnostic using unlabelled data. To this end, they consider the representation layer of a network to be probabilistic and derive a KL-divergence based regularizer to make the representations invariant to small input changes. They experimentally test their approach on VAEs and SimCLR SSL models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is fairly well-written and the high-level problem it studies is an important one. However, its biggest shortcoming in my view is that there is no evaluation of  whether representations learned using the proposed approach are truly robust in an  task-agnostic manner (which is their stated goal). In particular, the major draw of SSL methods is that their representations transfer to a vast variety of downstream tasks. However, all the experiments in this paper are focused on training on unlabelled data from a particular dataset (MNIST/CIFAR/ImageNet) and testing on the *same* dataset. To make the paper more convincing and aligned with the narrative in the abstract/introduction, the authors must demonstrate improved robustness on transfer tasks (e.g., the tasks in Kornblith et al [arXiv:1805.08974]). This is crucial because the method assumes (in prop1) that the xs for all tasks share the same support, which might not be true in practice. Note that Kim et al do study the performance of RoCL (the baseline) in this transfer setting (Table 4 in their paper). 

Additionally, the authors gloss over seemingly important details in their paper. For instance, there needs to be a more detailed discussion of:

- Exactly how the representations are made probabilistic (how do they get the mean/std), especially for SSL models like SimCLR.
- In S4.2, they state that the dimensionality of probabilistic representations is 2d. Are the baselines (AT/TRADES/RoCL) also trained with representations of size 2d? If not, simply having a bigger network could lead to better robustness of the proposed approach.
- In the VAE case, what is the downstream task? Is it classification on the learned representations?

Finally, the authors state that prior work hasn’t studied how well robustness transfers which does not seem to be the case. For instance, Kim et al study robust transfer in the SSL setting and Shafahi et al (ICLR 2020) do so in the supervised setting. Additionally, conceptually the approach is very similar to TRADES and a discussion of this is warranted in the main paper (as opposed to the appendix).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As mentioned above, certain key details are omitted from the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that the approach has promise, however the evaluation needs to be improved significantly to demonstrate that the learned representations are truly robust in a task-agnostic manner. The authors should also include evaluations for the l2 case to validate that the results generalize to other adversaries. I would be happy to improve my score if the authors include these evaluations and clarify the missing details.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies robust unsupervised representation learning by considering adversarial robustness. Specifically, by incorporating an adversarial regularizer into the unsupervised learning phase, the learned robust model can be more effective on downstream tasks. Applications of both the generative model (VAE) and the discriminative model (Contrastive learning) have been investigated. Extensive experiments on typical datasets have demonstrated that the proposed Urkle is more robust to adversarial attacks in the downstream tasks compared to well-known baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- This paper studies an interesting problem that has been rarely discovered: robust unsupervised learning. Given the practical capability of unsupervised learning, in my opinion, such a field is worth investigating.
- The proposed method is easy to implement and can be applied to a wide range of models, such as VAE and SimCLR which are demonstrated in the paper.
- The experimental results are promising, surpassing baseline methods by a large margin.

Weakness:
- First of all, the proposed method is quite simple, which means the technical contribution is limited. Moreover, the qualitative results illustrated in Figure 2 are not very significant. In my opinion, the left figure and right figure are pretty much the same.
- The choice of divergence measure shall be justified. Why KL divergence is used? Is it possible to use another divergence measure, say $\ell_1$ distance, to achieve comparable results?
- Moreover, the computation of adversarial data shall be explained more specifically. For VAE and SimCLR, what is the exact loss that is attacked to produce the adversarial examples? If I understand correctly, the attacked loss should be the original training loss of the corresponding method. To this end, by minimizing the KL divergence regularizer in Eq. 4, the claim that a lower bound is achieved in the downstream tasks is problematic. Because the adversarial robustness only corresponds to the unsupervised loss, rather than the supervised downstream tasks. Therefore, the claim “it will transfer directly to the downstream task and help minimize the bound in Eq. 4” shall be further justified.
- The hyper-parameter $\beta$ that decides the importance of the robustness regularizer shall be analyzed more specifically. Directly setting it to a specific value, and claiming “slightly increasing this value leads to even better representation” is not well-supported and unprofessional.
- The writing of this paper shall be further polished. It is not easy to follow the main storyline.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is moderate in clarity and quality. The proposed Urkle method has limited novelty. Implementation details are provided to ensure reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have carefully read the methodology and experiments. This paper studies an interesting problem and proposes an effective method, however, there are still some concerns (see weaknesses). If the authors can address my concerns, I will consider raising my score.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Training task agnostic robust representations is an interesting problem. The proposed solution uses a KL divergence based regularization term along with the traditional loss function.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Pros:

- The paper is written reasonably to understand and follow along.

- Use of KL divergence along with the contrastive or cross-entropy losses is interesting.

# Cons:

- Presentation can be improved greatly throughout the paper.

- Use of KL divergence in a loss function is not that novel in deep learning literature. However, its use as a regularizer for curbing adversarial attacks is a bit interesting.

- On the creation of these $x^{u\_adv}$ examples sounds same as creating some perturbed versions of two value tuples discussed. Why do we need these 4 valued tuples, can't you simple get away with the pairs of (x, x^{u\_adv})?

- The empirical evidence shown in the form of experiments is not sufficient. For example, after the pre-training in an unsupervised/self-supervised fashion, how long should one run in fine-tuning to achieve the reported results?

 ### Minor comments: 

 - There are some minor typos here and there that need to be fixed.

 - The literature does not seem to have been fully covered in the discussions in the paper. The formatting is also somewhat misaligned.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality: The presented approach or the presentation can be further improved but it is reasonable as it is.

Novelty: Use of KL divergence as a regularizer in combination with contrastive/ CE loss may not be all that novel as it already exists

Reproducibility: Some of the results might be reproduced however have clarity on method details and the experimental settings used would greatly improve the reproducibility
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is a nice attempt but not entirely convinced to believe the robustness mainly because of the concerns on the perturbations used, the use of KL divergence as a regularizer in unsupervised/SSL learning and the empirical evidence is not clearly explained. Therefore refraining from accepting it at this point.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to learn robust representations against adversarial attacks without running costly adversarial training (AT). The authors prove that the AT objective is upper bounded by a loss that can be minimized using the minimization of the downstream task (e.g. classification) and the minimization of a regularizer term which does not require real labels, e.g. it can be minimized in a self-supervised objective. Then, a number of experiments on standard image datasets are conducted to validate this point.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* [+] Adversarial attacks and the vulnerability of neural networks is an interesting topic. 

 * [+] The task of finding an alternative to the costly adversarial training is important. 

 * [-] The empirical validation is rather weak, e.g. it is not tested in various tasks and self-supervised tasks to claim task-agnostic structure. 

 * [-] The accuracies of the baselines seem reduced with respect to the accuracies reported in previous papers, e.g. in trades (CIFAR10 results). 

 * [-] The comparisons with limited data could also be compared with methods in the literature that are established for this purpose, i.e. robustness under limited data. However, no such methods are included, which makes the comparisons weak.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper aims to replace adversarial training with an alternative method capitalizing on the progress of self-supervised learning. The idea is clear, however I feel that currently there are few claims that are not fully supported. 

For instance, the method is claimed to be “task-agnostic” and “it can be straightforwardly applied to most of these self-supervised learning methods”, however only a single task is considered and one SSL method. I am not sure how this supports the claim that this is task-agnostic. 

One of the motivations for the proposed method is not to have to repeat the expensive AT for downstream tasks, however only a single task is considered here. So, again this weakens the argument of using the learned representations across tasks. 

In Fig. 2, is the plot a T-SNE? 

Why is the learning rate 1.2 in page 8? Isn’t this a bit high? 


*Minor points*: 

The introduction mentions that the proposed idea is equivalent to enforcing a low Lipschitzness, however the proposed metric is on distribution level (KL divergence) and not on the individual vector level, right? 

The paper requires proofreading as there are currently several issues: 

 * \citet{} should be used appropriately, e.g. in “(Alayrac et al., 2019) utilizes [...]”. 
 * After \citet{} typically plural should be used, e.g.  “Alayrac et al., 2019 utilize”. 
* “the robustness transferS” (page 4). 
* “exCiting” (page 5).
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe adversarial attacks are an interesting and significant topic. Finding an alternative to the AT is also a challenging task. However, I am concerned that the proposed alternative is not close to being a valid alternative that performs well, while there are several questions that are unclear by studying the manuscript.

content.title: Task-Agnostic Unsupervised Robust Representation Learning
content.abstract: It has been reported that deep learning models are extremely vulnerable to small but intentionally chosen perturbations of their input. In particular, a deep network, despite its near-optimal accuracy on the clean images, often mis-classifies an image with a worst-case but humanly imperceptible perturbation (so-called adversarial examples). To tackle this problem, a great amount of research has been done to study the training procedure of a network to improve its robustness. However, most of the research so far has focused on the case of supervised learning. With the increasing popularity of self-supervised learning methods, it is also important to study and improve the robustness of their resulting representation on downstream tasks. In this paper, we study the problem of robust representation learning with unlabeled data in a task-agnostic manner. Specifically, we first derive an upper bound on the adversarial loss of a prediction model (which is based on the learned representation) on any downstream task, using its loss on the clean data and a robustness regularizer. Importantly, the regularizer is task-independent, thus we propose to minimize it directly during the representation learning phase to make the downstream prediction model more robust. Extensive experiments show that our method results in a robust model for downstream tasks without any supervised adversarial training, and achieves preferable adversarial performance compared to relevant baselines.

content.TL;DR: We propose a method to learn robust representations without any labels or adversarial fine-tuning in downstream tasks, based on a theoretically grounded unsupervised robustness regularizer.
